“The translations of the Categories, the Analytics, and the Isagoge held in the Āṣafiyya Library under no. 668 are the work of Aḥmad ibn al-Muqaffaʿ.”
From all of this, we can conclude that translations or explanations of Aristotle’s works on logic existed before the age of al-Maʾmūn.
The existence of two manuscripts containing such material supports this conclusion. In other words, Arab-Islamic thought was already in contact with these works before al-Maʾmūn’s reign.
As for the age of al-Maʾmūn itself, Muslim historians agree that this was a period in which the translation of philosophical sciences flourished, with logic at the forefront.
Ṣāʿid even wrote that “the first of the philosophical sciences to receive attention were logic and astronomy.”
Some of the leading figures involved in the translation movement became known specifically for translating Aristotle’s logic.
Among them were Abū Nūḥ and Sallam, who lived during the reign of al-Maʾmūn.
Sallam was the first to translate Aristotle’s entire Organon into Arabic.
Later, in the same period, Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq, who lived from 877 to 909 CE, also translated the Organon.
From the age of al-Maʾmūn onward, the translation of works on logic into Arabic continued, together with the writing of explanations and commentaries.
At the same time, a struggle developed between supporters and opponents of logic among theologians and philosophers in the Arab-Islamic world.
This struggle was one of the historical forms taken by the wider ideological conflict of the period.
The philosopher and scientist al-Kindī was the first to write original works on logic in Arabic that were not translations or commentaries.

He wrote a treatise introducing logic and then another shorter version of it, a treatise on the ten categories, a treatise on guarding against the deceptions of the Sophists, and both a long and a short treatise on logical demonstration.

From this review of the historical evidence, we can conclude that it is difficult to identify precisely when Arab-Islamic thought first came into contact with Aristotelian logic, or with Greek logic more generally.
The matter is not simple enough to be settled merely by reading historical sources and references, comparing their texts, and deciding that one account is more convincing than another.
The problem is more complicated than this kind of secondary comparison can resolve.
As we have seen, the historical sources themselves are clearly inconsistent, both about the date of this first contact and about what exactly is meant by “contact” in the first place.
Where does this confusion come from?

Could it be because “much of what was translated in the eighth century—the second century AH—was lost, to the point that the earliest surviving translation dates from the ninth century, or the third century AH”?
We do not deny that this may help explain the confusion among historians.
But for our purposes, it is not enough.

Another question immediately presents itself: if so much translated material from the eighth century disappeared, why did all the translations of logic disappear, while at the same time most of the material translated from other fields survived—including Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ’s translations of Persian and Indian literature from the same century?

One possible answer would be this: perhaps this is reasonable evidence that logic was not actually translated until the ninth century. If anything had been translated earlier, at least some of it would probably have survived rather than all of it disappearing.
In our view, however, this answer is wrong because it does not fit the historical reality.
The actual development of Arab-Islamic society during the seventh and eighth centuries gives us evidence on this question that is difficult to dismiss.
That evidence comes close to showing directly that Arab-Islamic thinkers knew some of the main questions and basic rules of logic before the eighth century.
We have already pointed to some of the historical signs that support this conclusion. They form only part of the wider evidence.
If we now look at some of the most important cultural developments in that same society and period, we immediately encounter a well-known phenomenon.
The sciences usually described as the Arab sciences—language, literature, history, Islamic law, Qurʾanic commentary, hadith, and kalām—developed at an astonishing speed.
They moved visibly from simpler to more advanced forms, and from relative simplicity toward greater structure and complexity.
This was, in reality, the result of the historical interaction between the Arab conquerors and the other peoples of the young Arab empire.

Most of these peoples belonged to old and varied civilizations and cultures. At the time of the Arab conquests, some of them still preserved the heritage of those civilizations and cultures through forms of living practice.
One result of this vast interaction was that the method of Aristotelian logic entered into the heart of the Arab sciences themselves.
It is well known that the influence of logic on these sciences became so strong that logic eventually served as a reference point even for the rules of Arabic grammar.
This is particularly striking because grammar, as a purely linguistic discipline, might naturally be expected to resist the control of logical rules and structures.
At the time, this difference appeared clearly in one of the main divisions between two grammatical methods: the method of the Basra school and that of the Kufa school.
The Basra school became known for using logical analogy in deriving the rules of grammar.

The Kufa school, by contrast, became known for deriving grammatical rules from the actual speech of Arabic speakers in the desert. In other words, it returned to Arabic in its earlier forms, extending back to the pre-Islamic period.
For this reason, the grammarians of Basra became known as the “people of logic.”
That name has strong historical significance. It confirms that logic had already entered into a working relationship with the sciences of Arabic and Islam.
This influence also had conservative opponents.
Their hostility found expression in a famous saying from the second century AH:
This saying points us toward the same historical conclusion. It confirms that this relationship existed at an early stage.

The influence of logic could not have reached so deeply into Arabic linguistics and the Islamic sciences—which themselves were only emerging during the first century AH—unless at least a full generation had passed since the beginning of their contact with logic.
The appearance of the effects of logic within these sciences represents a qualitative change.
And a qualitative change cannot happen without enough gradual accumulation to prepare the way for it.
Such preparation also requires enough time for the transformation to take place.
As we have said, the relationship of influence between one science and another, one form of thought and another, or one culture and another is extremely complex.
For that reason, it can never be assigned a completely precise starting date.
There is another point worth considering.
De Boer was right when he said that the early use of logic by the people of Basra was no accident.
The influence of philosophical schools genuinely did appear in Basra before it appeared elsewhere.
Many of Basra’s grammarians were Shiʿis and Muʿtazilites, and they opened the way for “foreign wisdom” to influence their theological doctrines.
Why did the influence of philosophical schools appear in Basra before it appeared elsewhere?

Why were the Shiʿi and Muʿtazilite grammarians of Basra the first to open the way for “foreign wisdom to influence their theological doctrines,” even though the Shiʿa were more numerous and more concentrated in Kufa, where there were also grammarians and theologians just as there were in Basra?
And why did the Muʿtazila arise in Basra rather than in Kufa?
Earlier in this study, when discussing the problem of predestination, we laid the basis for answering these questions. Basra was the first centre in which that debate took root.
The point can be summarized by saying that throughout the Umayyad period, Basra was distinguished by two major features.

The first was that, more than any other Muslim city at the time, it contained a dense concentration of social forces and political parties both opposed to Umayyad rule and supportive of it, together with the competing intellectual movements that expressed these forces and parties.

This situation rested above all on the fact that Basra and its surrounding region had become a major centre in which large groups of working people were concentrated, including peasants, slaves, small traders, the destitute, and workers employed in craft industries. In Kufa, by contrast, we find the great merchants, major investors in land and agriculture, and the ruling aristocracy.

The second feature was this: because Basra brought together such sharply opposed social groups, it experienced some of the harshest forms of repression. This repression fell both on the forces of political opposition and on the poor and vulnerable working groups within society.

These social and political conditions made Basra especially ready—earlier and more strongly than other places—to absorb ideas and sciences that offered new ways of looking at society, nature, and thought. Such ideas made it possible to approach these questions with a more advanced kind of awareness. They also gave people an ideological weapon against the ideology of the Umayyad state, which insisted that there was only one path to knowledge and truth, and only one source of them. That approach left little room for people to use their own powers of understanding, especially human reason.

Logic therefore became the tool that organized the use of this new ideological weapon: the new philosophical ideas entering Umayyad society through the broad social and cultural interaction taking place within an empire made up of many different peoples.

But logic was also an ideological weapon in its own right. It offered a rational way of organizing the relationships between subjects and propositions and of reaching conclusions through the independent use of reason. Used in thinking, deduction, and the formation of general judgments, logic therefore became an indirect class weapon against another kind of weapon: transmitted texts and ready-made generalizations. The state used these to impose its absolute authority over the different forces within society and to fight both its political and its class opponents.
This was the ideological meaning of using logic in the Umayyad period, and the same basic meaning applied to philosophical thought more generally.

We therefore cannot imagine philosophical thought reaching the Arabs during the Umayyad period, as the historical evidence indicates that it did, while remaining separate from logic. The social and cultural channels through which philosophy reached them already combined philosophy and logic.

These channels included the Nestorian and Jacobite schools of Syria and Mesopotamia, the school of Alexandria, the mixing of civilizations among the peoples of the Arab empire, religious and intellectual debate, and the way material interests both came together and came into conflict within the concrete historical structure of material production. All of these social and cultural conditions carried philosophical thought and logic together. They did not bring one without the other.

As kalām gradually took shape, grew, and developed during the first and second centuries AH—first through the Qadarites, and later through their Muʿtazilite heirs—this development took place in the presence of both philosophical thought and its main rational tool at the time: logic.

The historical sources still do not tell us exactly how logic reached Arab thought during the Umayyad period or through what channel it arrived. But the loss of this particular historical link does not leave us without a method for reconstructing much of the path Arab thought was following as it developed alongside Arab society itself after the rise of Islam and the great conquests.

At the same time, we should not say that the historical sources deny that logic had reached Arab thought in this period. Nothing in them supports such a denial. Logic could already have had a direct and concrete effect on methods of thinking and on the development of Arab sciences, just as it could help arm political and class opposition with a new intellectual weapon in the ideological struggle.

As we have already seen in this chapter, the sources provide more than a few clues from which this can reasonably be inferred. For that reason, it is no longer very important for our argument whether logic reached Arab-Islamic thought through direct translation, through the spontaneous mixing of civilizations, or through a looser and less organized form of intellectual exchange.
3 — The Role of Logic in Arab-Islamic Thought

Earlier in this chapter, we tried to shed some light on the relationship between Arab-Islamic thought and Aristotelian logic, as part of the wider development of its relationship with Greek philosophical knowledge.

Seen in this light, we can perhaps understand the social and ideological meaning of that relationship. It formed part of a much larger historical change: the movement of Arab thought away from the conditions of its earlier stage in the pre-Islamic period—a stage of simple, direct, and spontaneous thinking—and toward its first forms of combined, analytical, abstract, and more complex thought. In other words, toward the first beginnings of philosophical awareness.
During the long course of this change, throughout the first two centuries AH, Arab thought gradually developed a need for a clear rational method.

It was encountering many kinds of knowledge that were new to it, differing in form, subject, and cultural origin. It needed a method that could guide its use of this knowledge, help develop it, and enrich it through its own experience.

This was necessary in order to meet the needs of a large and rapidly changing new society. Many different social forces were developing within it, including active forces located in the society’s material production. Here we are especially concerned with those who worked the land and those involved in craft production.

This society, with its predominantly feudal but distinctive character, increasingly required more advanced techniques in these crafts. It also demanded new and technically sophisticated products to satisfy the growing luxury of the aristocracy, represented increasingly by state officials at the many levels of the political and administrative hierarchy.

All these needs together helped produce the organized and openly sponsored translation of philosophical and natural sciences, mathematics, and medicine at the beginning of the third century AH, the ninth century CE. The state itself now supported this movement.

It was almost an explosion of activity after the long period of preparation that had taken place during the previous two centuries. And, as historians of the translation movement generally agree, almost the whole of Aristotle’s logical tradition stood at the forefront of it.
Against this historical explanation, Ibn al-Nadīm gives us an idealist and highly personal explanation in the Fihrist. Some historians later repeated it without question.
According to the author of the Fihrist, the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn:

“Saw Aristotle in a dream and asked him a number of questions. When he awoke, he ordered that Aristotle’s books be translated. He wrote to the Byzantine emperor asking permission to send for whatever books of the ancient sciences he wished to obtain from Byzantine lands. The emperor eventually agreed after first refusing. Al-Maʾmūn then sent a group that included al-Ḥajjāj ibn Maṭar, Ibn al-Biṭrīq, Salm, the head of the House of Wisdom, and others. They took what they found and selected what they wanted. When they brought the books back to him, he ordered them to translate them, and they did.”
A similarly crude explanation is often given for the scientific translation movement under al-Manṣūr Abū Jaʿfar.

Even many modern historians explain his use of the school of Jundishapur, its doctors, and its teachers—and the growing demand for relatively advanced medicine, trained physicians, and further translations of Greek and Arabic medical books—by pointing to an illness suffered by the caliph himself.

They tell us that al-Manṣūr developed a stomach disorder and that his doctors advised him to summon Jurjīs ibn Bukhtīshūʿ, the Syriac head of the physicians of Jundishapur, to treat him. He was dramatically brought to court, as the story is usually told. When his treatment succeeded, al-Manṣūr persuaded him to remain in Baghdad permanently. This then supposedly became the beginning of a vigorous new movement in medical treatment, medical research, and medical writing—and so the story continues.

In reality, all the scientific translation and intellectual and cultural activity that took place under al-Manṣūr and al-Maʾmūn, as well as before and after them, was part of the wider development of society.
It reflected historical necessities that had been maturing within that society itself. The internal and external conditions needed for these developments were gradually coming together.

We have said that Aristotle’s logical works stood at the forefront of the translation movement in philosophy, natural science, and mathematics during the Abbasid period of al-Maʾmūn. Historians of this movement are generally agreed on this.

Does this mean that Arab-Islamic thought consciously chose Aristotle’s logic as the method it needed at this stage of development—a method that could guide the organization of its different intellectual activities and provide what al-Fārābī described as:

“The laws whose function is to correct the mind and guide a person toward what is right and true in everything where reason may fall into error; the laws that preserve and protect the mind from mistakes, slips, and errors in matters of reason; and the laws by which we test conclusions where we cannot be sure that someone has not made a mistake…”?
It is not easy to answer this question with certainty.

There can be no doubt that Aristotle’s logic had a deep influence on the development of Arab-Islamic thought as it moved toward philosophical awareness and later began to construct its own philosophical systems.

But there is equally little doubt that Arab-Islamic thinkers—especially those working in philosophy, natural science, and mathematics—continually adapted this logical system to the questions placed before them by their own complex and changing society.
